news_title: Researchers assess antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella
efet_title: Researchers assess antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella
efet_body:
Scientists have identified certain antimicrobial resistance traits likely to spread through China’s food chain over the next 25 years.
Research by King’s College London and the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (China CDC) analyzed genetic traits linked to antimicrobial resistance in drug-resistant Salmonella across China’s food chain.
China is one of the largest producers and consumers of meat, so understanding how Salmonella and its resistance genes move through the chain could have implications for global food safety, said scientists.

news_title: Tomato use suspended as Italy tackles Salmonella outbreak
efet_title: Tomato use suspended as Italy tackles Salmonella outbreak
efet_body:
Another Italian region has stopped the serving of uncooked tomatoes in selected sites after reports of Salmonella infections.
A notice from authorities in Emilia-Romagna ordered a ban on the use of cherry tomatoes that have not undergone cooking by all private and public foodservice providers in schools, social care facilities, hospitals, and nursing homes.
Officials said action was taken based on the precautionary principle and to ensure maximum public health protection while investigations continue. Measures will apply until further notice. Anyone found breaching the order could face prosecution.
Infections linked to tomatoes
In several European countries and various Italian regions – including Emilia-Romagna – cases of salmonellosis caused by monophasic Salmonella Typhimurium and Salmonella Strathcona were detected during 2024, 2025, and 2026.
These cases have been linked, through epidemiological, microbiological, or genomic evidence, to the consumption of raw cherry and datterini tomatoes.
In Emilia-Romagna, surveillance of Salmonella infections in the region between 2024 and 2026 has identified 112 cases caused by Salmonella Strathcona and five monophasic Salmonella Typhimurium infections.
The notice referenced two outbreak assessments by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) in 2024 and 2025, as well as several notifications on the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF) platform.
Officials in Emilia-Romagna said the complex traceability of fresh tomato supply chains makes it difficult to identify the operators involved and product distribution details.
National and international impact
On Sept. 30, 2026, a national task force was convened. Experts found that recent outbreaks in Puglia, Lombardy, Lazio, and Friuli-Venezia Giulia were linked to fresh tomatoes contaminated with monophasic Salmonella Typhimurium sequence type 34 or Salmonella Strathcona sequence type 2559.
Authorities in Puglia had earlier suspended the serving of raw fresh tomatoes in food preparation centers and distribution points for institutional catering. This included nurseries, schools, social care and healthcare facilities, residential care homes and hospitals. Measures followed a rise in Salmonella Strathcona infections and detection of Salmonella in a batch of tomatoes from Caltanissetta.
Since July 2026, more than 160 infections have been recorded in 10 European countries.
In Austria, 21 confirmed and eight
probable Salmonella Strathcona
cases have been reported in seven federal states. The Robert Koch Institute (RKI) said recently that there are 39 patients associated with the outbreak in Germany since June. People are also sick in Denmark, France, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.
In late 2025, testing in Austria detected the outbreak strain in organic cherry tomatoes from Italy. The outbreak strain was also previously found in the irrigation water of a tomato producer in Sicily.

efet_title: Trader Joe's wraps named as source of ongoing E. coli outbreak - USA Today
efet_body:
FOOD
Food Safety
Add Topic
Trader Joe's wraps named as source of ongoing E. coli outbreak
Mary Walrath-Holdridge
USA TODAY
Oct. 23, 2026
Updated Oct. 24, 2026, 12:45 p.m. ET
Hear this story
The source of an ongoing E. coli outbreak that has sickened at least 50 people was chicken wraps sold at Trader Joe's, federal health authorities confirmed.
The Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) confirmed the link in an email to USA TODAY on Friday, Oct. 23, following a
USA TODAY story about a lawsuit and investigation related to the outbreak.
The lawsuit, along with state investigation documents reviewed by USA TODAY, named Trader Joe's Tarragon Chicken Salad Wraps as the source.
Trader Joe's confirmed in an Oct. 20 email to USA TODAY that it pulled its Tarragon Chicken Salad Wraps from shelves in 9 states after the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) notified the chain in September that there may be a "possible issue" with them.
"The
E. coli
O157:H7 outbreak (2026-04) investigation identified ready-to-eat, multi-ingredient chicken wraps from certain Trader Joe’s stores as a common exposure among people who became sick," FSIS said in its statement. "The wraps reported by some cases very early in the investigation were proactively removed from the market by Trader Joe’s before a link to the outbreak was established."
The Food and Drug Administration, along with the USDA, had previously identified the source of the outbreak only as an unnamed "Ready-To-Eat Multi-ingredient wrap with chicken." The public
FDA
and
FSIS
entries for the outbreak still listed the unspecified wraps as of Friday, Oct. 23.
The USDA is still working alongside other agencies to investigate the ingredient that was the source, it said, and "extensive product testing" has all been negative. It is unlikely to be chicken, it added, as chicken is rarely the source of the outbreak strain of E. coli (E. coli O157:H7), also known as Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, or STEC, a type of foodborne illness that sometimes causes a serious condition that can lead to kidney damage called hemolytic uremic syndrome.
Historically, health agencies like the FDA and USDA have named multi-ingredient products during associated outbreaks, even if a specific ingredient within wasn't yet identified as the culprit. In this case, FSIS said the products were removed from shelves before a link could be confirmed and a recall could be initiated.
"FSIS quickly issues information to the public through recall releases and public health alerts when a product is linked to illnesses and there is actionable information for consumers. If an ongoing public health risk is identified, the agencies will take appropriate action," the statement read.
Food attorney Bill Marler, who is representing two women who say they became ill after eating the wraps in a lawsuit against Trader Joe's, told USA TODAY that he believes the FDA and USDA should have named the source publicly, even if products were pulled from shelves.
"The only thing that FSIS is hanging its hat on is that the product's off the shelf; there's no reason to tell anybody anything," he said. "But when they can identify the product or the processor or the grower, they should be open and tell the public. The public has the right to know."

news_title: Judge delays USDA's reorganization plan - Food Safety News
efet_title: Judge delays USDA's reorganization plan - Food Safety News
efet_body:
A federal judge has stopped the USDA from a reorganization that was to close some offices, cut some staff and relocate some others. The stay is in effect for at least two months.
The department’s reorganization efforts stopped Cyclospora research at the Agricultural Research Center just prior to the nation’s largest-ever cyclosporiasis outbreak this summer.
The action by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California is in response to a lawsuit filed by unions representing government employees. The lawsuit contends that the USDA’s plans illegally reprogrammed congressional appropriations. Such action can only be taken by Congress.
“Congress did not contemplate USDA using its appropriated funds to shut down offices or relocate employees,” the unions’ motion states. “To the contrary, Congress was actively working to restrict the agency’s ability to do so.”
The court order stalling the USDA’s action runs through Dec. 11. That is the expiration date of the action passed by the U.S. House of Representatives to keep government funded.
When the continuing resolution to keep government operations funded expires, the USDA can attempt to convince Congress not to kill its reorganization plans.
The USDA’s initial reorganization plans were revealed in July 2025. The department announced more plans in April this year, which included the closing of some offices and other facilities. The plans will also require hundreds of employees to relocate from Washington D.C. to offices across the country, which unions say will result in the resignations of hundreds of employees.
Although the reorganization is billed as a way to reduce the number of USDA offices, the reorganization plan calls for a new National Food Safety Center in Urbandale, IA. Under the reorganization plan, the department’s Food Safety and Inspection Service would be moved to the Urbandale office.
Another new facility included in the reorganization plan would house the Agricultural Research Service’s Agricultural Research Center (BARC), now located in Beltsville, MD. The plan calls for the relocation of research programs and employees to facilities across the country, including a new Science Center in Athens, GA.
Other offices and staff that the reorganization plan would relocate include the National Institute of Food and Agriculture, the Economic Research Service, and the National Agricultural Statistics Service. All of those operations are under the Research, Education, and Economics (REE) umbrella.
Some senators have expressed concern about the plans for the REE operations, raising questions about decreased capacity and the further deterioration of the USDA’s ability to conduct research. Reports on federal employment data since the beginning of the Trump Administration show that the USDA has lost a significant number of employees — in FY 2025 and the beginning of FY 2026,
USDA lost more than 20,000 staffers
, many of whom held advanced degrees and were veteran employees with valuable technical expertise.

news_title: Raw Oysters Salmonella Outbreak Sickens 55 People - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_title: Raw Oysters Salmonella Outbreak Sickens 55 People - Food Poisoning Bulletin
efet_body:
The
CDC
counts 27 people sick in 12 states in the Salmonella Telelkebir outbreak linked to raw oysters harvested from the Little Wicomico River in Virginia. Five of them have been hospitalized and no deaths have been reported, according to CDC’s October 19 notice. CDC says their illnesses began between May 29 and September 14, 2026. We first reported the outbreak at 27 cases
on October 20
.
On October 21, the
Virginia Department of Health
counted 55 cases in 19 states in a wider Salmonella Telelkebir investigation, and this post first reported that number. VDH’s page, updated October 22, no longer gives it. VDH now says CDC is focusing its investigation on a genomic subgroup of 27 cases from 12 states, and that there are additional Salmonella Telelkebir cases beyond those 27. Other states and federal partners are investigating those cases, and VDH says the source of those illnesses has not yet been determined.
Of the 27 people in CDC’s group, 10 reported eating raw oysters, and shellfish tag and traceback information is available for seven of them. Two ate oysters from a single source, in Virginia. The other five ate oysters from more than one source. For each of them, one possible source was the same Virginia growing area, and VDH lists their other sources as Virginia, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Georgia/Canada, or Virginia/New Jersey/Massachusetts. VDH says raw oysters from a single Virginia harvest area, the Little Wicomico River, are the likely source of the illnesses in this group.
CDC and FDA linked the outbreak to raw oysters harvested by the Little Wicomico Oyster Company from the Little Wicomico River in Virginia. They were the only oysters in common to the seven sick people included in traceback, according to VDH. The company recalled shellstock oysters harvested from September 18 through October 8, 2026. The
FDA
says they were distributed to restaurants and retailers in California, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, Missouri, North Carolina, New Jersey, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Texas and Virginia, and may have been distributed further. VDH collected oysters from the river on October 13 and again on October 21 for testing, and says the genetic test results are pending.
Salmonella can lead to hospitalization, especially for young children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems. If you or someone in your family was hospitalized after eating raw oysters, the
Salmonella lawyers at Pritzker Hageman
can answer your questions about this outbreak.
If you ate oysters and have been ill with the
symptoms
of a Salmonella infection, especially if the oysters came from the Little Wicomico River, see your doctor. You may be part of this outbreak.

Listeria monocytogenes
(
Lm
).

Lm
can cause listeriosis, a serious infection that primarily affects older adults, persons with weakened immune systems, and pregnant women and their newborns. Less commonly, persons outside these risk groups are affected.
